title: Entryway Paint Colors: 5 Wall Colors in One Entry
description: One entryway, five Sherwin-Williams wall colors from Alabaster to Naval, with codes, hex values, light reflectance and a note on what to check before you paint.
dek: Same door, window, console and floor. Only the wall color changes. Compare five on screen, then sample the two you like on your own wall.
hook: A paint chip is small, and an entry wall is the first one you see. This guide shows one entryway with the same white six-panel door, window, oak console, round mirror and plank floor in five Sherwin-Williams wall colors, so the wall is the only thing that changes.

The images are AI-generated concept pictures, not photos of a real entryway. The code, hex value and light reflectance for each color come from Sherwin-Williams' own color pages, read Oct 25 and Nov 18, 2026. A screen only shows a closest match, never the paint itself, so test a sample on your own wall before you buy a can.
gallery_intro: Light reflectance (LRV) runs from 0 to 100, and lower numbers mean a darker color. The five run from Naval at 4 to Alabaster at 82. The ceiling stays warm white in every look and the door and trim keep their original color.
gallery_note: AI-generated concept images of one entryway. Colors are on-screen approximations of the paint listed under each look, so test a sample on your wall. They are not photos of a real entryway.

compare_title: The five colors at a glance

compare.name: Alabaster
compare.note: Warm white. Little contrast with the trim, so the entry reads light and open.

compare.name: Naval
compare.note: Very dark. Can swallow light in a small entry, so check it at night under your own bulb.

compare.name: Agreeable Gray
compare.note: A soft greige. Closest to the original wall, so it is the hardest of the five to tell apart on a screen.

compare.name: Cavern Clay
compare.note: A warm terracotta. Reads more orange in bright light and browner in shade.

compare.name: Evergreen Fog
compare.note: A muted gray-green. Can read gray on a cloudy day and greener in warm light.

tips.h: Sample on the wall, not on a chip
tips.p: Paint a patch about two feet square on your own entry wall and look at it in the morning, at midday and at night under your own bulb. An entry often has little daylight, so the color can shift a lot.

tips.h: Check it next to your trim and door
tips.p: The concept images use warm white trim and a white door. If yours are bright white or a different tone, hold the sample next to them, since the same color can look warmer or cooler beside each.
The floor in these images is a warm medium oak. Cool colors like Naval and Evergreen Fog read cooler against warm wood, and Cavern Clay reads warmer. Hold the sample near your own floor.

tips.h: Match the paint to the wall
tips.p: Entry walls take scuffs from bags and shoes. Check the can or the color page for the finish, and ask the store which sheen the maker suggests for a high-traffic wall.

Wipe off dust and scuff marks, patch holes and let it dry before you paint. Check the can for the recoat time and the number of coats the maker suggests, since dark colors over a light wall can need more.

final: If you do one thing, sample your top two colors on the wall itself and look at them at three times of day. A color that wins on a screen can lose in your own light.
skipped: Paint, primer and brushes sold by the can, since the right product depends on your wall and the maker's directions.

Product links, since this guide is about the color choice.
how_picked: The five colors cover a warm white, a dark blue, a greige, a terracotta and a gray-green, so you can compare very different directions in one entry.
Codes, hex values and light reflectance were read from the Sherwin-Williams color pages on Oct 25 and Nov 18, 2026.
The wall is recolored on one image in code, so the door, window, console, mirror and floor stay the same in every look.
how_note: The images are AI-generated concept pictures and show how a color might read, not how paint will look on your wall.
